claims.text: The formation and persistence of a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide above 900 °C is governed by lattice matching at the alloy/oxide interface.
Al-containing CrFeCoNiX compositions promote formation of a sub-stoichiometric, coherently bonded alumina-rich or chromium-rich oxide.
A coherently bonded oxide minimizes alloy/oxide interfacial stresses.
Reduced interfacial stress produces controlled oxide growth and resistance to cracking and spallation.
CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn variants do not provide the same alloy/oxide lattice compatibility as an Al-containing variant.
The lower lattice compatibility predicted for Si- or Mn-containing variants makes their oxides more prone to cracking and spallation.
At elevated temperature, diffusion of reactive elements, notably Al, leads to formation of an oxide whose lattice parameters closely match those of the HEA substrate.
Close lattice matching reduces thermal stresses and prevents oxide crack initiation.
Insufficient lattice matching in alloys with higher Si or Mn contents causes faster oxide growth.
Faster oxide growth generates stresses that induce cracking and spallation.
CALPHAD modeling and in situ HTXRD can be used to predict oxidation kinetics and phase stability.
An optimal Al content or reactive-element balance will produce a slow-growing oxide that remains intact during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Si- or Mn-dominated variants will exhibit faster oxide growth, greater residual stress, and more cracking or spallation than the favorable Al-containing variant.
Vacuum treatment minimizes oxidation and can help distinguish oxidation-driven changes from purely thermal or mechanical changes.
The proposed comparison applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys in single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution conditions, either as-cast or heat-treated, without pre-formed oxides.
The proposed service and exposure window is 900–1100 °C for at least 10 hours in an oxidizing or corrosive atmosphere.
A lack of composition-dependent differences in oxide coherence or stability would falsify the proposed link between X-element-controlled lattice coherence and oxide stability.
